opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is that when you compare models trained on wildly different amounts of data, you're not really comparing like with like, and the leaderboard format hides that. If one model has seen a few hundred million words and another has seen a trillion tokens, and the second one does better on some benchmark, what have you learned? Maybe the architecture is better, maybe the training objective is better, or maybe it just saw a lot more examples that look like the test items. You can't disentangle those explanations from a single number.

For the questions I care about, which are often about human language acquisition and generalization, that's a real problem. A child gets maybe tens of millions of words of input in the first several years of life. So if a model needs a thousand times more data than that to reach some level of grammatical competence, that tells you something quite different than if it gets there with a human-scale amount. The amount of data is part of the result, not a nuisance variable you can ignore.

There's also the contamination issue, and more subtly, the issue of what counts as generalization. With enormous training sets, it gets increasingly likely that something very close to your test items, or the patterns they're probing, appeared in training. So a high score might reflect something closer to memorization or interpolation than the kind of abstraction we're trying to measure. With smaller, controlled training sets you have a much better handle on what the model has and hasn't been exposed to.

So what I've argued for is that we should think of data quantity as a dimension of the evaluation itself. Ideally you'd report performance as a function of training data, compare models at matched amounts of data, and treat sample efficiency as something we're explicitly trying to improve. That's part of the motivation behind efforts like the BabyLM challenge, where everyone trains on a fixed, developmentally plausible amount of data, so differences between systems actually reflect differences in inductive biases and learning algorithms rather than who had access to the biggest corpus and the most compute.

r001.rationale: The response says enormous training sets make it more likely that test items or the patterns they probe appeared in training, so a high score may reflect memorization or interpolation rather than generalization.

r002.rationale: It discusses abstraction and generalization broadly, but does not explain that interpreting unfamiliar combinations of familiar sentence components requires composing their meanings under limited training.

r003.rationale: It notes that test patterns may occur in large training sets, but does not state that a structure unfamiliar to a human may already have appeared in a model’s trillions of words of training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the issue is really about what question you're trying to answer. When you put, say, BERT or GPT-3 head to head against a model that was trained on a tiny fraction of the data, and you ask which one does better on some syntactic evaluation, the answer is almost always going to be the bigger model. That's not very interesting. It just tells you that more data helps, which we already knew.

The question I'm actually interested in is a question about learning. Humans acquire language from a relatively modest amount of input, maybe tens of millions of words by the time a child is ten or so, and they end up with pretty robust syntactic generalizations. So if I want to use language models as a way of thinking about human language acquisition, or as a way of asking what inductive biases are needed to learn syntax, then the amount of data is a critical variable. A model trained on a hundred billion words is just not in the same regime as a child. If it learns subject-verb agreement, that doesn't tell me much about whether the architecture has the right biases, because it may have simply memorized or seen so many examples that it never needed the right bias.

So when people compare across models trained on wildly different amounts of data, they're conflating two things: the architecture's inductive biases, and the brute force of data. If you want to separate those, you have to control the data. Train the models on the same corpus, ideally one that's closer to human-scale, and then look at the differences. Then the differences in behavior are actually attributable to the model and not to the fact that one of them read the entire internet.

There's also a more mundane methodological point, which is that these benchmarks were often constructed with particular models in mind, and the training data for big models frequently overlaps with the test material in ways that are hard to audit. So the head-to-head comparison can be unfair in ways that aren't even about data quantity in the abstract. But the main thing for me is really about what you learn from the comparison. If you're doing engineering, fine, compare whatever you want and pick the best model. If you're doing cognitive science, the data budget is part of the experimental design, and you can't just ignore it.

r001.rationale: The response says a large model may learn syntactic patterns by memorizing or seeing many examples, confounding the effect of data quantity with its inductive biases.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning syntax and inductive biases, but does not say that understanding unfamiliar combinations of familiar sentence components requires composing their meanings under limited training experience.

r003.rationale: It mentions large models reading the internet and possible test-data overlap, but does not state that a structure unfamiliar to a human may already have appeared in training on trillions of words.

astra-6.text:
Well, it depends on what you’re trying to learn from the comparison. If you just want to know which system performs best on a particular task, then comparing them on the same dataset makes sense. But if you want to know whether one architecture is better at learning language than another, the amount of training data is a confound. A model might do better simply because it’s seen much more data, rather than because it has a better way of learning from that data.

And that’s particularly important if we’re interested in these models as models of human language acquisition. If a system needs vastly more input than a child receives to achieve similar performance, then matching that performance doesn’t, by itself, explain how children learn language. So you want to control the amount of data, or look at performance across different amounts of training data, rather than just compare the final scores.

r001.rationale: The response says greater training-data exposure can explain better performance, but does not identify memorization as the confound or connect it specifically to evaluating generalization.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss composing meanings of familiar sentence components to understand unfamiliar combinations under limited training experience.

r003.rationale: It does not mention human-unfamiliar sentence structures or that they may have appeared in a model’s trillions of training words.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it depends on what you’re trying to learn from the comparison. If you just want to know which system performs better on a particular task, then that’s a perfectly reasonable thing to do. But if you want to draw conclusions about which model has a better learning mechanism, the amount of training data is a confound. One model might do better simply because it’s seen much more data, rather than because its architecture is better suited to learning language.

That’s especially important when we compare language models with humans. If a model needs vastly more linguistic experience than a child to reach the same performance, then matching that performance doesn’t establish that it learns language in the same way. So we should look at how well models learn given comparable amounts of data, and ideally at their learning curves, rather than just comparing their final scores.
